newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ex-French Socialist treasurers deny breaking law.
newsitem.headline: Ex-French Socialist treasurers deny breaking law.

text.p: Two former treasurers of France's Socialist Party charged with running an illicit party fundraising scheme denied acting illegally at their trial on Monday, saying party finance laws were ill-defined at the time.

Henri Emmanuelli and Andre Laignel said they bore a political responsibility for schemes to funnel funds to the party via a consultancy firm dating back to the late 1980s, but maintained they had not broken any laws.
"I fully accept the existence of these consultancy companies. They took part in financing the Socialist Party," Emmanuelli, who was treasurer from 1988 until 1991, told the court.

"I thought in taking up the post that there was fraud, but I was not shocked," he added. "How can one pass from a political level to a criminal one, when we were in a period that lacked laws? It's a historical anachronism."
Emmanuelli, who also served as head of the Socialist Party from 1994-95, has already been convicted on similar charges in an earlier trial which took place in Brittany in 1995.

Emmanuelli was given a one-year suspended prison sentence and a 30,000 franc ($6,000) fine in May 1995 for receiving illicit campaign contributions from a front company known as the Urba consultancy company which was run by party insiders.
Emmanuelli is on trial for handling stolen goods and for influence peddling and Laignel is on trial for complicity in the same charges.
Laignel, treasurer from 1981-88, used the same defence as Emmanuelli, saying that laws had since been tightened.
"No political party could carry out its task simply with members' donations," Laignel said. "There was no personal enrichment. In seven years, I never signed a cheque, my role was political."
In the earlier trial, investigators uncovered a covert funding network used by the Socialists to finance their campaigns by taking rake-offs from public works contracts via front companies like Urba.
The front companies allegedly demanded consulting fees from companies seeking public tenders, and part of that money was then funnelled to local Socialist candidates and the national party.

The trial, that began on March 3 and is expected to last a month, is based on similar accusations, again involving the Urba consultancy firm, but this time involving party operations in the Mediterranean port city of Marseille.
Prosecutors say the party illegally raked off 9.4 million francs ($1.65 million) from public works contracts awarded in the region during 1988 and 1989.
